overview: The exercise compared storage layouts using small virtual disks. I used Windows software volumes to observe the capacity trade-offs between striping, mirroring and distributed parity.

steps.title: Attach the lab disks
steps.description: I used the VMware hardware settings to add seven small virtual disks while keeping the operating system disk separate.

steps.title: Initialize the new disks
steps.description: I opened Disk Management, selected the added disks and initialized them. The captured dialog has GPT selected; partition style is separate from the striped, mirrored or parity-based volume layout.

steps.title: Start a striped volume
steps.description: I selected two disks for a striped RAID 0 volume, combining their capacity for the exercise.

steps.title: Format and convert the striped disks
steps.description: I assigned the volume label and drive letter, formatted it with NTFS and accepted the basic-to-dynamic disk conversion required by the wizard.

steps.title: Inspect the striped result
steps.description: I checked the striped volume’s Healthy status and its two-disk layout in Disk Management.

steps.title: Create the mirrored volume
steps.description: I used two different disks for RAID 1. The wizard retained approximately one disk of usable space because the second disk holds the mirror.

steps.title: Create the RAID 5 volume
steps.description: I combined the remaining three disks in a RAID 5 volume with distributed parity, assigned its label and drive letter and formatted it with NTFS.

steps.title: Review the completed volume layout
steps.description: I inspected the final Disk Management view and compared the striped, mirrored and parity-based layouts and their reported status.

checks.title: Disk and volume configuration
checks.description: The captures show added disks, the selected partition style, stripe and mirror setup and the final volume layout.

checks.title: Capacity comparison
checks.description: The mirror wizard visibly retains one disk of usable capacity when two disks are selected.

lessons: RAID 0 combines capacity but has no disk-failure redundancy.
RAID 1 trades usable capacity for a second copy; three-disk RAID 5 reserves the equivalent of one disk for parity.
RAID does not replace backup, and a Healthy status is not a failure-recovery test.
scope: The lab demonstrates configuration and capacity trade-offs on virtual disks. It contains no measured throughput benchmark or captured disk-failure/rebuild test. Dynamic disk layouts are documented as the curriculum exercise, not as a new production storage recommendation.
